cards.title: What OWASP Is — and What It Isn't
cards.teaser: The OWASP Top 10 is the most-cited document in application security, yet it is widely misused. It is a risk-awareness document, not a compliance checklist — and confusing the two is one of the field's most common mistakes.

runs.text: The Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) is a nonprofit foundation whose mission is to improve software security through open-source tools, standards, and community-driven research. Its best-known output is the
OWASP Top 10

, a ranked list of the ten most critical web application security risks. The list has been published since 2003 and is revised roughly every three years; the 2021 edition remains authoritative as of 2026.

The methodology behind the rankings combines two inputs: data from hundreds of organizations covering millions of tested applications, and a community survey of security practitioners rating emerging risks. This hybrid approach is why the 2021 list added categories (Insecure Design, SSRF) that had limited historical CVE data but were rated as high-severity by practitioners.
OWASP uses a standard risk-scoring model for each category. The score is a product of two axes:

items.text: — how easy is it to exploit? How widespread is the vulnerability?
— what is the technical and business consequence of a successful exploit? Data breach, service disruption, full system compromise?

runs.text: What the Top 10 is
not

: it is not a complete security standard, not a penetration test scope, not a compliance framework, and not a substitute for threat modeling. Fixing all ten categories does not mean an application is secure — it means the application avoids the ten most common failure patterns. The PCI DSS, ISO 27001, and NIST 800-53 frameworks reference the Top 10 as a baseline, but the Top 10 explicitly discourages treating it as a checkbox exercise.

OWASP maintains related projects for context: the ASVS (Application Security Verification Standard) for systematic verification, the WSTG (Web Security Testing Guide) for testing methodology, and the SAMM (Software Assurance Maturity Model) for organizational maturity. The Top 10 is the entry point; these are the practice guides.

The OWASP Top 10 is a ranked awareness document showing the ten most dangerous patterns attackers exploit. Think of it as a "most-wanted" list for web app risks — it tells you where to look first, not everything you need to do.

cards.title: A01: Broken Access Control
cards.teaser: The number-one risk on the 2021 list: when users can act outside their intended permissions. IDOR, missing authorization checks, and JWT manipulation are the canonical patterns — and the Capital One breach shows the real-world cost.

runs.text: Broken Access Control moved from fifth place in 2017 to first in 2021, appearing in 94% of tested applications. It covers any situation in which the application fails to enforce what authenticated users are permitted to do — not
who
they are (that is authentication) but
what
they can access.
The three dominant attack patterns:

items.text: — the API exposes resource IDs directly in URLs or request bodies. Changing
retrieves another user's order. The fix is server-side ownership checks on every resource access — never trust the client-supplied ID without verifying the requesting user owns that resource.

— admin endpoints are hidden from the UI but accessible via direct HTTP requests. Obscurity is not access control. Every endpoint must enforce its own authorization, independently of whether the UI renders a link to it.
— forging or tampering with JSON Web Tokens to escalate privileges. Classic attacks include setting the algorithm to
(the server accepts unsigned tokens), or changing the
claim in a token whose signature is not verified server-side.

runs.text: Real-world example: the
Capital One breach (2019)

exposed 100 million customer records. The attacker exploited a misconfigured web application firewall to reach an internal metadata endpoint (SSRF, covered in A10) and then used an overpermissioned IAM role to access S3 buckets — a broken access control failure at the cloud infrastructure layer. The role had read access to far more buckets than the application required.

The primary mitigation for A01 is to deny access by default and require explicit grants. Implement authorization checks server-side on every request, log access control failures, and alert on repeated failures — they are reconnaissance signals.

Broken Access Control means a user can do things the app wasn't supposed to let them do — read someone else's data, call admin functions, or forge their identity in a token. It's the top risk because it's everywhere and the consequences are severe.

cards.title: A02: Cryptographic Failures
cards.teaser: Formerly named 'Sensitive Data Exposure,' A02 was renamed in 2021 to focus on root cause: weak or missing cryptography is what exposes the data. Plaintext storage, weak TLS, and broken cipher suites are the failure modes.

runs.text: The renaming from "Sensitive Data Exposure" to "Cryptographic Failures" was deliberate. Exposed data is the symptom; failed cryptography is the disease. The category covers failures that lead to sensitive data being readable by attackers — in transit, at rest, or in processing.
Critical failure patterns:

items.text: — passwords stored as plain text or with reversible encoding (Base64 is encoding, not encryption). Passwords must be hashed with a memory-hard algorithm: Argon2id (preferred), bcrypt, or scrypt. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken for password hashing — they are fast, which is precisely the wrong property.
— TLS 1.0 and 1.1 are deprecated (RFC 8996, 2021). SSLv3 and SSLv2 are critically broken. Use TLS 1.2 minimum, TLS 1.3 preferred. Validate certificate chains; do not disable certificate verification.

— CBC mode ciphers without HMAC, RC4, DES, 3DES, and export-grade ciphers all have known weaknesses. Use AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Check cipher suite configuration with tools like testssl.sh or Qualys SSL Labs.
— serving any page or API endpoint over HTTP allows network attackers to intercept traffic. Use HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) to prevent protocol downgrade and cookie hijacking.

runs.text: The
Adobe breach (2013)

is the canonical A02 case: 153 million user records were stolen, with passwords encrypted using 3DES in ECB mode — a reversible cipher that also leaked password patterns due to ECB's deterministic block structure. Identical passwords produced identical ciphertext, enabling statistical attacks.

Data classification is the prerequisite: know which data is sensitive (PII, credentials, financial records, health data) before deciding what protection it needs. Not everything requires encryption, but everything that does requires it consistently — no exceptions for convenience or performance.

Cryptographic Failures means the app uses bad or missing crypto — storing passwords in plain text, using outdated TLS, or picking broken cipher suites. The consequence is sensitive data readable by attackers who shouldn't see it.

cards.title: A03: Injection
cards.teaser: Injection vulnerabilities occur when untrusted data is sent to an interpreter as part of a command or query. SQL injection is the archetype, but NoSQL, command, LDAP, and template injection all follow the same pattern. Chapter 3 covers injection in depth.

runs.text: Injection was the top OWASP risk for over a decade before dropping to third place in 2021. The fundamental pattern is invariant: an application constructs a query or command by concatenating attacker-controlled data with trusted syntax, and the interpreter cannot distinguish between data and instructions.
The injection taxonomy:

items.text: — the classic. Unsanitized user input inserted into SQL queries. Mitigation: parameterized queries or prepared statements. String concatenation is never acceptable. ORMs help but do not eliminate risk if raw query escapes are used.
can be injected via JSON bodies. Passing
as a password field can bypass login. Validate input types and reject unexpected operator keys.
— user input passed to shell commands (
). Allows arbitrary command execution. Avoid shell invocation entirely; use language-native APIs. If unavoidable, use allowlist validation, never blocklist.
— unescaped user input in LDAP filter strings. Can enumerate directory entries or bypass authentication filters.

runs.text: The
Heartland Payment Systems breach (2008)

— 130 million credit card numbers stolen via SQL injection — remains one of the costliest injection attacks on record. The principle behind all mitigations is structural separation: never build queries by string concatenation; always use mechanisms that structurally separate data from syntax.

Injection is covered in depth in Chapter 3, including SQLi mechanics, blind injection, time-based inference, second-order SQLi, and ORM pitfalls. This card provides the Top 10 context; that chapter provides the exploitation and defense detail.

Injection happens when user input gets treated as code instead of data. In SQL injection, crafted input escapes the data context and becomes part of the SQL command. The fix is structural: use parameterized queries so data can never become syntax.

cards.title: A04: Insecure Design
cards.teaser: New in 2021, Insecure Design recognizes a failure class that code review and pen testing cannot fix after the fact: security was never considered during requirements and architecture. You cannot patch your way out of a fundamentally insecure design.

runs.text: A04 is categorically different from the other nine items on the list. A SQL injection vulnerability is an implementation flaw — it can be fixed in a single parameterized query. An insecure design flaw is structural: the system was architected without security requirements, and correcting it requires rethinking the design.
OWASP defines Insecure Design as the absence of security controls that should have been present in the design phase. Examples:

items.text: Missing rate limiting on credential recovery
— if the password reset flow has no attempt limits, an attacker can enumerate the entire user base or brute-force OTP codes. This is a design requirement that cannot be retrofitted trivially.
No segregation of duties in privileged workflows
— a payment system that allows a single user to both create and approve wire transfers. The design must require two separate principals for sensitive operations.
— microservices that trust all traffic on the internal network without service-to-service authentication. When one service is compromised, lateral movement is trivial.
— no one asked "what is the worst thing an attacker could do with this feature?" during design. Security requirements were not derived; they were assumed.

runs.text: The practical response to A04 is integrating security into the design phase via
threat modeling

. The STRIDE framework (Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information Disclosure, Denial of Service, Elevation of Privilege) provides a systematic way to enumerate threats for any design. OWASP's own Threat Dragon is a free tool for this. The goal is to surface security requirements before a line of code is written.

A04 is the hardest category to address because it requires organizational change, not just code change. Security must be a requirement in sprint planning, architecture review, and design documents — not an afterthought in the security review gate before release.

Insecure Design means security was never considered when the system was architected. The difference from other bugs: you can't patch a design flaw — you have to redesign. The fix is threat modeling before code is written, not after.

cards.title: A05: Security Misconfiguration
cards.teaser: The most broadly applicable category: misconfiguration covers default credentials left in place, verbose error messages leaking internals, missing security headers, and debug interfaces exposed in production. The Verkada camera breach shows how widespread this is.

runs.text: A05 is the attack surface that exists before any custom code is written. It includes insecure defaults in web servers, application frameworks, cloud platforms, databases, containers, and network devices. Security misconfiguration is notable because it is frequently the fault of operations and deployment processes, not developers.
The major subcategories:

items.text: — admin/admin, root/root, admin/password. Shodan indexes millions of devices with unchanged defaults. Every credential must be changed at provisioning time; default credentials must never reach production.

— stack traces, SQL queries, internal paths, and framework versions sent to the client. This is reconnaissance data. Production must return generic error messages; full errors go to server-side logs only.
are browser-enforced defenses against XSS, clickjacking, MIME sniffing, and protocol downgrade. All should be present on every response.
), PHP info pages, Django debug mode. These expose configuration secrets and enable remote code execution.
— publicly readable S3 buckets and Azure Blob containers. Misconfigured cloud storage is responsible for more data breach records than all other misconfiguration forms combined.

runs.text: The
Verkada breach (2021)

exposed live feeds of 150,000 security cameras. The attacker found a superadmin username and password exposed in a Jenkins build script. Classic default/hardcoded credential exposure — A05 combined with A02.

The mitigation strategy for misconfiguration is hardened build pipelines: use Infrastructure as Code with security linting (tfsec, cfn-nag), enforce security headers via middleware, scan for exposed cloud storage continuously, and build security into deployment templates rather than fixing instances by hand.

Security Misconfiguration is everything insecure about how a system is set up rather than coded — default passwords left unchanged, verbose errors telling attackers your framework version, admin panels open to the internet. It's the attack surface that exists before your first line of custom code.

cards.title: A06: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
cards.teaser: Using libraries with known CVEs is the organizational equivalent of leaving a patched-over door. The Equifax breach — 147 million records lost via an unpatched Apache Struts vulnerability — is the canonical A06 case.

runs.text: Modern applications are predominantly composed from third-party dependencies. A typical Node.js application has 500-1000 transitive dependencies; a Java Spring Boot application can pull in hundreds of JARs. Each dependency is a potential CVE entry waiting to be exploited.

A06 covers the risk of running software with known, publicly disclosed vulnerabilities. The CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System) score rates severity from 0 to 10; critical vulnerabilities (CVSS 9.0+) are exploited in the wild within days of disclosure.
The attack surface and mitigation:

items.text: — integrate SCA (Software Composition Analysis) tools into CI:
, Dependabot, Snyk, OWASP Dependency-Check. Fail the build on critical CVEs; alert on high.
— direct dependencies are the easy case. Transitive dependencies (dependencies of dependencies) are where vulnerabilities hide. Tools like
and OWASP Dependency-Track walk the full dependency graph.

— a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) in CycloneDX or SPDX format documents every component in the build. Executive Order 14028 (2021) required SBOMs for US federal software; the practice is spreading to regulated industries.

— know your mean time to patch (MTTP) for critical CVEs. Elite security teams patch critical vulnerabilities within 24-72 hours. A patching process that requires six weeks of change management for a critical library is a systemic risk.

runs.text: The
Equifax breach (2017)

exposed 147 million people's personal data. The vector was CVE-2017-5638, a critical Apache Struts 2 vulnerability with a patch available for two months before exploitation. Equifax's asset inventory did not include the affected server; the patch was never applied.

The Equifax lesson is not just "patch faster" — it is "know what you're running." You cannot patch components you don't know exist. Complete and continuously updated software inventory (SBOM) is the prerequisite for effective vulnerability management.

A06 is running library versions with published security holes that attackers already know how to exploit. Equifax lost 147 million records because a vulnerable library sat unpatched for two months. The fix: continuous dependency scanning and a fast patching process.

cards.title: A07: Identification and Authentication Failures
cards.teaser: Formerly 'Broken Authentication,' A07 covers credential stuffing, session fixation, weak passwords, and missing MFA — the attacks that let adversaries become authenticated users. Chapter 4 covers auth in depth.

runs.text: A07 covers the failures in confirming that a user is who they claim to be, and in maintaining that assurance across a session. The category dropped from first place in 2017 to seventh in 2021, partly due to wider adoption of managed identity providers — but it remains critical, particularly for applications that implement authentication themselves.
The primary attack patterns:

items.text: — using username/password combinations from prior data breaches (billions of credentials are available in breach databases like HaveIBeenPwned) against other services. Effective because users reuse passwords. Mitigation: MFA, breach-credential detection, rate limiting, CAPTCHA.
— systematic password guessing, enabled by missing rate limiting, missing account lockout, or weak password policies. Any login form without attempt limits is vulnerable.

— an attacker supplies a known session ID before login; if the server does not rotate the session ID upon successful authentication, the attacker's pre-authentication session becomes an authenticated session. Always issue a new session ID on login.
— long-lived tokens without expiry, session IDs in URLs (appear in logs and referrer headers), missing

runs.text: The
Rockstar Games breach (2022)
and the
Uber breach (2022)

both involved social engineering combined with MFA fatigue attacks — bombarding users with push authentication requests until they approve. Multi-Factor Authentication is necessary but not sufficient; phishing-resistant MFA (FIDO2/WebAuthn hardware keys) is the gold standard.

The strongest mitigation for A07 is to not implement authentication yourself. Use a battle-tested identity provider (Auth0, Okta, Cognito, Keycloak) that handles session management, MFA, and breach-credential checking. Authentication is too complex and too critical to build in-house for most applications. Chapter 4 covers the full surface.

Identification and Authentication Failures means the app can't reliably verify who users are — or can't maintain that assurance once verified. Credential stuffing exploits password reuse; session fixation hijacks logins. The answer is MFA plus strong session hygiene.

cards.title: A08: Software and Data Integrity Failures
cards.teaser: New in 2021, A08 covers trust violations in the software supply chain and data pipelines — insecure deserialization, CI/CD pipeline compromise, and auto-update mechanisms that don't verify package integrity. SolarWinds is the defining breach.

runs.text: A08 merged the 2017 category "Insecure Deserialization" with a broader concern that OWASP identified as increasingly critical: integrity failures across the entire software delivery chain. The question it asks is: does the application verify that the code and data it processes haven't been tampered with?
Two major subcategories:

items.text: — applications that deserialize objects from untrusted sources (HTTP bodies, cookies, message queues) without integrity checks. Java's native serialization, Python's pickle, and PHP's unserialize have long histories of remote code execution via crafted payloads. Mitigations: prefer JSON over binary serialization formats; validate and sanitize before deserializing; never deserialize from untrusted sources into live objects without type constraints.

— CI/CD pipelines that pull unverified packages from registries, that don't sign or verify build artifacts, or that run arbitrary code from third-party GitHub Actions without pinning to a commit hash. Dependency confusion attacks (registering a package in a public registry with the same name as an internal package) exploit this pattern.

runs.text: The
SolarWinds SUNBURST attack (2020)

is the defining A08 breach. Attackers compromised SolarWinds' build pipeline and injected malicious code into the Orion software update, which was then cryptographically signed by SolarWinds and distributed to 18,000 customers including US federal agencies. The attack was undetectable by signature verification because the signature was legitimate — the integrity failure was in the build process itself.

Mitigations for A08: pin GitHub Actions and external dependencies to specific commit hashes rather than mutable tags; verify package checksums (lock files, Sigstore); sign build artifacts; audit your CI/CD pipeline's own access controls; implement SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts) framework controls.

Software and Data Integrity Failures means your app processes code or data it hasn't verified came from a trustworthy source and wasn't tampered with. SolarWinds shows the extreme: attackers got into the build pipeline, signed malware with a legitimate cert, and shipped it as an update.

cards.title: A09: Security Logging and Monitoring Failures
cards.teaser: You cannot respond to a breach you cannot see. A09 covers the absence of logging for security events, missing alerting, and failure to detect attacks in progress — the gap that turns an incident into a months-long dwell-time disaster.

runs.text: The 2021 OWASP data survey found that this category is difficult to test for using automated tools — its presence is felt most acutely after a breach, when investigators discover the logs needed to reconstruct the attack either don't exist, were not retained, or were deleted by the attacker.
What must be logged:

items.text: — successful and failed logins, with timestamp, IP, and user agent. Failed login bursts are credential stuffing. Successful logins from new geographies are account takeover signals.
— every denied access attempt, especially repeated attempts. Repeated 403 responses against different object IDs is IDOR reconnaissance.
— rejected inputs that match attack patterns (SQL syntax in fields, script tags, null bytes). These indicate active exploitation attempts.
— privilege escalation events, password changes, administrative actions, data exports. Every action that changes the security state of the system.

runs.text: The
Marriott/Starwood breach (2014-2018)

is the A09 case study: attackers had access to the Starwood reservation database for four years before discovery in 2018. The breach exposed 500 million guest records. Adequate monitoring and anomaly detection on data access patterns would have detected the persistent exfiltration far earlier.

Beyond logging, A09 includes the alerting and response side. The IBM Cost of a Data Breach Report consistently shows that organizations with security monitoring and incident response capabilities have dramatically lower breach costs and shorter dwell times. The industry average dwell time (attacker presence before detection) was 207 days in 2021; organizations with mature monitoring cut this to weeks.

Logging anti-patterns: logging passwords or sensitive data in application logs (GDPR violation and new exposure); logs stored only on the same server they protect (attacker deletes evidence); no log retention policy (logs rotated before forensics need them); alerts that fire so frequently they are ignored.

Security Logging Failures means your app doesn't record enough information to know when you're being attacked or to reconstruct what happened after a breach. Marriott had an attacker in their database for four years. Good monitoring means detecting that in days, not years.

cards.title: A10: Server-Side Request Forgery (SSRF)
cards.teaser: New to the Top 10 in 2021 and added purely on community survey merit, SSRF tricks the server into making HTTP requests on the attacker's behalf — enabling cloud metadata exfiltration, internal service access, and port scanning from inside the network.

runs.text: Server-Side Request Forgery exploits the server's trusted position within the network. When an application fetches a URL supplied by the user (for a webhook, image preview, file import, or PDF renderer), an attacker can supply an internal URL — and the server, trusted by the internal network, faithfully fetches it.
The primary SSRF targets in cloud environments:

items.text: (AWS/GCP/Azure). The metadata endpoint returns IAM credentials, instance configuration, and user data scripts. The Capital One attacker used SSRF to reach this endpoint, retrieved IAM credentials, and used them to exfiltrate S3 buckets. AWS now requires IMDSv2 (session-oriented metadata requests) to prevent SSRF metadata theft, but IMDSv1 is still commonly in use.
— microservices that trust traffic from within the VPC. An SSRF vulnerability in any public-facing service becomes a pivot point into the internal network.
with various port numbers to map the internal network topology via timing differences in responses.

runs.text: Mitigations:

items.text: to known-good domains. Deny all private IP ranges (
— DNS rebinding attacks can bypass IP-based allowlists. Validate the resolved IP, not just the hostname.
— use IMDSv2, restrict outbound traffic from application servers with egress firewall rules, and segment internal services so they require authentication even from internal callers.

runs.text: SSRF is covered in depth in Chapter 6, including blind SSRF, DNS rebinding bypasses, and protocol smuggling variants. This card establishes the Top 10 context.

SSRF means the attacker gets your server to make web requests on their behalf. Because your server is trusted inside your network, they can reach things users can't — like the cloud metadata endpoint that hands out IAM credentials, as happened at Capital One.

cards.title: OWASP API Security Top 10
cards.teaser: APIs present a distinct attack surface that the web application Top 10 doesn't fully address. OWASP maintains a separate API Security Top 10 — last updated in 2023 — covering broken object-level authorization, mass assignment, and excessive data exposure.

runs.text: As web applications shifted from server-rendered HTML to JavaScript frontends backed by REST and GraphQL APIs, the attack surface changed. APIs expose data structures directly, are typically stateless, and are often consumed by mobile apps and third parties — introducing risk patterns not captured by the traditional web Top 10.
The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) highlights API-specific risks:

items.text: — the API equivalent of IDOR. Every API endpoint that operates on objects must verify the requesting user owns or has permission for that specific object. BOLA is the most prevalent API vulnerability.
API3: Broken Object Property Level Authorization

— returning more object fields than the caller should see (excessive data exposure), or allowing writes to fields the caller should not be able to modify (mass assignment). The fix: explicit response serialization; never pass raw ORM models to API responses.
— missing rate limits, missing pagination limits, or allowing queries that produce unbounded results. APIs must enforce per-client rate limits and result size caps.
) on sensitive endpoints, debug endpoints in production, HTTP verb inconsistencies.
— old API versions left running, shadow APIs, or undocumented endpoints. An API catalog and active version deprecation policy are required.

runs.text: The
Peloton API exposure (2021)

is a clean API3 example: the ride-metrics API returned full user profile data (age, location, weight, workout history) without authentication. Any unauthenticated caller could retrieve data for any user ID.

The relationship between the two lists: the web Top 10 covers the application layer broadly; the API Top 10 zooms into patterns specific to API design. Most API vulnerabilities are specializations of web Top 10 categories, but BOLA and mass assignment are distinct enough to warrant API-specific treatment.

The API Security Top 10 is the cousin list focused on REST and GraphQL APIs. The biggest risk (BOLA) is IDOR for APIs: your API hands back any user's data if you know their ID, because it never checks you're allowed to see it.

cards.title: OWASP ASVS — Measuring Security Systematically
cards.teaser: The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard turns the Top 10 risk awareness into a structured verification framework with three levels of rigor — the tool organizations use to answer 'how secure is this application, really?'

runs.text: The OWASP Top 10 answers "what are the most common ways applications fail?" The OWASP Application Security Verification Standard (ASVS) answers a different question: "what security controls should a given application have, and have they been verified?" It is the bridge between awareness and assurance.

ASVS is organized into 14 control categories (authentication, session management, access control, cryptography, error handling, data protection, communications, malicious code, business logic, file I/O, API, configuration, and more) and three verification levels:

items.text: — verifiable through automated testing: DAST scanners, fuzz testing, and basic penetration testing. Appropriate for low-value applications. Covers the Top 10 broadly. Pen test or automated scan is sufficient evidence.

— verifiable through code review plus testing. Appropriate for most business applications handling sensitive data. Requires access to source code and architecture documentation. The level most PCI DSS and HIPAA-regulated applications should target.

— appropriate for critical applications: financial systems, healthcare infrastructure, safety-critical software. Requires formal documentation of the security architecture, threat model, and code-level evidence for every control.

runs.text: The ASVS is used in three primary contexts:

items.text: — as a checklist of security requirements that should be captured as acceptance criteria during development. Teams select the appropriate level and map ASVS requirements to user stories.
— external pen testers can use ASVS to define a standardized scope rather than relying on ad hoc tester judgment. This makes assessments repeatable and comparable across engagements.
— buyers of third-party software can require ASVS Level 2 or Level 3 compliance as a contractual requirement, standardizing vendor security expectations.

runs.text: ASVS version 5.0 was released in 2025 with significant restructuring, including a new Cryptography chapter reflecting post-quantum guidance and expanded API security controls. When referencing ASVS requirements, always specify the version — v4.0 and v5.0 numbering is not backward compatible.

ASVS is the verification layer on top of the Top 10: instead of just knowing the risks exist, it gives you a structured checklist of controls to implement and test, at three levels of rigor. Think of the Top 10 as the syllabus and ASVS as the exam.

cards.title: Reading the Risk Scores — How OWASP Ranks Threats
cards.teaser: OWASP's risk methodology turns qualitative threat descriptions into comparable scores using two axes: likelihood (prevalence × detectability × exploitability) and impact (technical × business). Understanding the math reveals why the rankings shift between editions.

runs.text: The OWASP risk rating methodology is derived from the NIST risk methodology and adapted for web applications. Each Top 10 category receives scores on two primary dimensions, each composed of sub-factors:

items.text: — (1) Prevalence: how widespread is this vulnerability class across applications? (2) Detectability: how easily can automated scanners find it? (3) Exploitability: does exploitation require skill and specialized tools, or can a script kiddie exploit it with a Metasploit module?

— (1) Technical impact: what can an attacker do after successful exploitation — read data, modify data, execute code, crash the service? (2) Business impact: what is the financial, reputational, regulatory, and privacy consequence to the organization?

runs.text: This methodology explains the major ranking shifts between 2017 and 2021:

items.text: rose from A05 to A01 because prevalence data showed it present in 94% of applications — the highest of any category. Despite moderate exploitability (requires application knowledge), sheer prevalence drives the composite score up.
dropped from A01 because prevalence decreased — parameterized query libraries are now standard in most modern frameworks — even though impact remains critical.

entered on community survey merit alone: prevalence data was insufficient, but security practitioners rated the business impact of cloud-environment SSRF (metadata credential theft, lateral movement) as severe enough to warrant inclusion.

runs.text: The practical implication: OWASP rankings are not universal. An application that runs on-premises with no cloud metadata endpoints has a lower SSRF risk than a cloud-native application. The Top 10 is a statistical baseline across the industry, not a risk ranking for your specific application — threat modeling (A04's core concept) is required to calibrate risk to context.

OWASP publishes the raw data used to compile each Top 10 edition at github.com/OWASP/Top10/tree/master/2021-Data. The 2021 dataset included 544,000 applications from 29 contributing organizations. Reviewing the data methodology is the best antidote to treating the list as scripture.

OWASP scores each risk by multiplying how likely exploitation is (how common is the bug, how easy to find and exploit) by how bad the outcome is (data loss, code execution, regulatory fine). That math is why the rankings shift between editions and why the list is a statistical industry baseline, not a personal risk score for your app.
